passage:
I'm Naveen, and I said the wrong thing at my friend Divyansh's grandfather's funeral. We were standing outside the hall, and Divyansh looked so lost. I wanted to help, so I blurted, "At least he lived a long life."
Divyansh's face closed. "Yeah," was all Divyansh said, and turned away to a cousin.
I felt sick for days. Later my older sister told me that those phrases, "at least" and "it was meant to be", usually make people feel unheard. She said, "Just say 'I'm so sorry' and 'I'm here'."
The next week I sent exactly that. Divyansh replied, "Thanks. That helped more."

qa.q: What did Naveen say outside the hall?
qa.a: Naveen said, "At least he lived a long life."

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling in the days after speaking at the funeral?
qa.a: Naveen felt sick with regret, realising the well-meant words had landed badly. Divyansh's closed face and the turning away made that clear.

qa.q: What did Naveen change the next week, and what happened?
qa.a: Naveen sent "I'm so sorry" and "I'm here", as the older sister suggested. Divyansh replied that it helped more.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt hearing "At least he lived a long life"?
qa.a: Divyansh probably felt unheard and hurt, since the loss was still fresh. The closed face and short "Yeah" show it did not comfort.

grounding: A teenager tells a grieving friend "at least he lived a long life," which hurts, and learns "I'm so sorry" and "I'm here" work better.

passage:
Teacher's note, Tuesday. Meher, class 10, has been absent for a week after her uncle's death. Today she returned. At break I heard Neelam, a classmate, say to her, brightly, "Everything is for the best, you know." Meher stared at her tray, and her eyes filled.
I waited until Meher had gone and spoke to Neelam privately. I said her intention was kind but that those words often sting. We practised two others: "I'm so sorry" and "I'm here if you want to sit together." Neelam went back at lunch and said just that. Meher nodded and moved her tray over.
Vandana, class teacher

qa.q: What did Neelam say to Meher at break?
qa.a: Neelam said, "Everything is for the best, you know."

qa.q: What did Neelam mean to do by saying "Everything is for the best"?
qa.a: Neelam wanted to comfort Meher and felt kind but awkward, not knowing better words. The teacher said the intention was kind.

qa.q: What did Vandana do that helped Neelam?
qa.a: Vandana spoke privately after Meher left, said Neelam's intention was kind but the words sting, and practised "I'm so sorry" and "I'm here if you want to sit together". Neelam then said it at lunch.

qa.q: What might Meher have been feeling when staring at her tray with filling eyes?
qa.a: Meher was probably hurt and grieving, feeling the words dismissed the loss. Staring down and tearing up suggest it stung.

grounding: A teenager tells a grieving classmate "everything is for the best," which stings, and a teacher helps them find kinder words.

passage:
Friday
Sarika came back to school today after her Nanaji's funeral. At lunch, Mehul said to her, "Well, at least your Nanaji was really old. He had a good long innings." He meant it kindly, I think. Then Tanya added, "Everything is part of God's plan."
I watched Sarika's face. She smiled, but her jaw went tight and she put her roti back in the box. She didn't say anything for the rest of lunch.
I didn't know what to say either. After school, walking to the gate, I just said, "Sarika, I'm so sorry about your Nanaji. I'm here if you want to talk, or not."
She stopped and hugged me. She said, "Thank you for not telling me it's fine."
I keep thinking about Mehul's face. He'll never know it hurt. Should I tell him? Maybe I will, gently.
Yash

qa.q: What did Mehul say to Sarika at lunch?
qa.a: He said, "Well, at least your Nanaji was really old. He had a good long innings."

qa.q: What was Yash feeling while watching Sarika at lunch?
qa.a: Yash felt uneasy and unsure, noticing Sarika's hurt but not knowing what to say.

qa.q: Why did Yash's words work better than Mehul's and Tanya's?
qa.a: Yash simply said sorry and offered to be there without explaining the death away, so Sarika didn't have to pretend it was fine.

qa.q: How did Sarika experience Mehul's and Tanya's words?
qa.a: Sarika felt hurt and alone, forcing a smile while her jaw tightened and she stopped eating.

grounding: A teenager observes friends offer well-meant phrases to a grieving classmate that hurt, and offers simple sorrow and presence instead.

passage:
The whole Class 11 of the small-town school went to Ojas's house after his father's funeral. They sat on durries in the courtyard, uneasy.
Baljeet watched as Harpal patted Ojas's shoulder and said, "Everything is God's will, yaar. He's in a better place now." Another boy added, "At least you have your mother."
Ojas nodded, but his hands were clenched on his knees, and he stared at the ground.
Baljeet felt his stomach turn. The words sounded right, but Ojas looked like he'd been hit.
When the others left, Baljeet stayed. He sat next to Ojas on the step and said only, "I'm so sorry, Ojas. I'm here."
Ojas didn't answer for a while. Then, very low, "Everyone keeps saying better place. I want him here."
"I know," Baljeet said. They sat until the lamps were lit.

qa.q: What did Harpal say to Ojas?
qa.a: Harpal said, "Everything is God's will, yaar. He's in a better place now."

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling as he watched Ojas?
qa.a: Baljeet felt uneasy and sick, his stomach turning as he saw the well-meant words hurting Ojas.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who doesn't know what to say to a grieving friend?
qa.a: Say simply that you are sorry and that you are there, then stay and listen, as Baljeet did, instead of explaining the loss.

qa.q: What were the well-meant words like for Ojas?
qa.a: They hurt Ojas, who clenched his hands and felt unheard, because he did not want a better place, he wanted his father back.

grounding: A teenager observes classmates' well-meant phrases hurt a grieving friend, and offers simple sorrow and presence.

passage: In the corridor of the Bristol sixth-form college, Xin watched Amara come back after a week away. Her grandad had died. Jordan got to her first, bright and loud. "Hey, at least your grandad had a really long life, yeah? And it all happens for a reason, right?" Amara's smile froze. Her hand tightened on her bag strap, and she said, "Yeah. Thanks," in a flat voice before walking fast towards the toilets. Jordan shrugged at Xin. "What? I was being nice." Xin wasn't sure what to say either. At lunch Xin found Amara alone on the bench by the art block and sat down. "I'm so sorry about your grandad. I'm here, if you want company." Amara was quiet for a long moment. Then she said, "He taught me to ride a bike," and started to cry, and Xin stayed.

qa.q: What had Amara's grandad taught her?
qa.a: He taught her to ride a bike.

qa.q: What was Xin feeling after Jordan said "I was being nice"?
qa.a: Xin felt unsure and uneasy, having seen Amara's smile freeze but not yet knowing what to say instead.

qa.q: Which words helped Amara, and why?
qa.a: "I'm so sorry about your grandad. I'm here" named the loss without explaining it away, so Amara felt safe to share a memory and cry.

qa.q: What did Jordan's words seem like to Amara?
qa.a: They seemed to brush past her grief, so her smile froze and she hurried away rather than show how hurt she was.

grounding: Shows a teenager noticing how a classmate's well-meant "long life" and "it all happens for a reason" hurt a grieving friend, while a simple "so sorry, I'm here" helps.
